readerTitle: Same shop, different owner: why who runs the idea matters
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점, 동네 가게 세 곳, 소프트웨어 아이디어) + 실제 관찰 (초기 투자자들이 창업자를 함께 평가하는 관행)
insight: 아이디어는 혼자 평가할 수 없다. 같은 아이디어도 누가 하느냐에 따라 전혀 다른 베팅이 된다.
misconception: 좋은 아이디어는 누가 해도 좋은 아이디어다. 열정만 있으면 그 시장에 맞는 창업자다.

sources.text: 모든 가게와 인물, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'founder-market fit'이라는 용어가 투자자 Chris Dixon에게서 널리 퍼졌다는 점(블로그 글 'Founder/market fit', 2013년경)을 게시 전에 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 "commonly credited to"로만 적었습니다.
초기 투자자가 매출이 없는 단계에서 창업자를 크게 본다는 내용은 일반적인 관찰로만 썼고, 특정 수치나 조사 결과는 인용하지 않았습니다.
3번 카드의 '첫 주 고객 15곳', '6개월', 8번 카드의 '정비소 사장 30명' 등은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: Same shop, different owner
body: It's 6:45 a.m. at a small hardware store. A plumber walks in, and before he says a word, the owner slides a box of fittings across the counter. She knows his jobs, his brands and his schedule.
Two blocks away, a newer store with the same shelves is half empty. Same products. Same street. A different person behind the counter.

image.label: Hardware store owner handing a plumber a box of fittings at dawn
image.brief: 이른 아침 동네 철물점. 카운터 뒤 주인이 작업복 입은 배관공에게 부품 상자를 미리 건네는 장면. 창밖은 해 뜨기 직전 푸른빛. 따뜻하고 익숙한 분위기. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Three shops. Which would you open?
body: You have savings for one small business in your town. Three options are on the table.
Which gives you the best chance?

options.text: A specialty coffee-bean shop. You love coffee and brew at home every day
options.feedback: Your enthusiasm will carry you through long days. But loving the product teaches you little about suppliers, margins or who actually buys beans.

options.text: A supply shop for local bakeries. You drove flour deliveries for eight years and know most bakers in town
options.feedback: It's the least exciting option, but you already know the customers, their problems and how to reach them. You start where others spend a year getting to.

options.text: A bubble tea shop. It's the fastest-growing category in your area
options.feedback: A growing market helps, but you'd learn everything from scratch while rivals who already know the trade compete for the same customers.

cards.title: The boring shop had a head start.
body: Picture all three a year in. The bakery supply shop signed its first 15 customers in week one. Its owner already knew who ran out of butter on Fridays and which bakers paid late.
The bubble tea owner spent six months learning what rivals already knew: which suppliers cut corners and what rent the foot traffic could carry.
The coffee-bean shop was well loved, but thin on profit. Enjoying coffee had not taught its owner much about selling it.

image.label: Three shopfronts, one busy with delivery crates
image.brief: 세 가게가 나란히 있는 거리 일러스트. 가운데 제빵 재료 가게 앞에 배달 상자와 손님이 많고, 양옆 버블티 가게와 원두 가게는 한산함. 과장 없이 담담한 톤. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Founder-market fit
body: **Founder-market fit** is how well a founder's knowledge, connections and commitment match the market they're entering.

It means an idea is never a bet on its own. The same shop is a safer bet in the hands of someone who already understands its customers. The term is commonly credited to investor Chris Dixon, and many early-stage investors now use it.

image.label: Founder and market as two puzzle pieces that fit
image.brief: 두 개의 퍼즐 조각 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 조각은 "Founder", 오른쪽 조각은 "Market". 맞물리는 돌기 부분에 "Insight", "Access", "Staying power" 라벨. 단순하고 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Fit has three parts.
body: When a founder fits a market, it usually shows up in three ways.
list: **Insight:** you know things about customers that outsiders learn slowly, or never
**Access:** you can reach the first customers, suppliers and partners
**Staying power:** you care about this market enough to stay through the dull, hard years
cards.callout: Passion alone covers only the third.

cards.title: Same idea, different bet.
body: Picture two people building identical booking software for dental clinics. One ran a clinic's front desk for ten years. The other has never been inside one. The first knows which screen the receptionist hates. The second has to find out.
This is why early-stage investors often ask **"Why you?"** before "Why this?". With no sales yet, the founder is much of what there is to judge.

cards.title: Fit can be built, and it can blind you.
body: Fit is not something you're born with. Many founders build it by working in an industry first, or by serving customers by hand for months before quitting their jobs.
Insiders have blind spots too. Years in a market can make "that's how it's always done" feel like a law.
And fit never replaces demand. The perfect founder for a market where nobody pays will still struggle.

cards.title: Now it's software.
body: You're a software developer with savings for one year of building. You have three ideas.

options.text: A task tracker for software teams. You are the user yourself
options.feedback: Your insight is real, but thousands of developers share it, and the market is crowded. Fit helps most where few others have it.

options.text: A parts-ordering app for auto repair shops. Your family runs one, and you know about 30 shop owners
options.feedback: You bring rare insight and your first users on day one. You'll trade some glamour for a head start few rivals can match.

options.text: An app for a hot new trend you've read a lot about, with no customers you know
options.feedback: You'd move fast on timing but start with no insight or access, racing people who live in that market.

cards.title: Judge the idea and the founder together.
body: Before asking whether an idea is good, ask whether you are the right person to run it.

**Try it today:** write your idea at the top of a page. Under it, list what you know that outsiders don't, the first ten people you could call, and why you'd still care in year five. A short list is your homework.
